t.1.16.1: Then Mandara, the best of mountains, adorned with mountain peaks shaped like the crests of clouds and covered with a network of creepers...
t.1.16.2: That mountain echoed with the cries of many kinds of birds and teemed with many kinds of fanged beasts, and it was frequented by Kiṃnaras and Apsarases, and even by the gods.
t.1.16.3: It rises eleven thousand yojanas high, and it is rooted below the earth in just as many thousands of yojanas.
t.1.16.4: Then all the hosts of the gods, unable to lift it up, approached Viṣṇu as he sat, together with Brahmā, and spoke these words.
t.1.16.6: "So be it," said Viṣṇu together with Brahmā, O Bhārgava. Then mighty Ananta rose up, urged on by Brahmā and also instructed by Nārāyaṇa for that task.
t.1.16.5: May you two here form a supreme resolve that leads to the highest good, and let an effort be made to uproot Mandara for our welfare.
t.1.16.7: Then, O brahmin, the mighty Ananta forcibly uprooted that king of mountains, together with its forests and the creatures that dwelt in those forests.
t.1.16.8: Then the gods, together with him, approached the ocean and said to it, "For the sake of the amṛta we shall churn your waters."
t.1.16.9: Then the Lord of the Waters said, "Let there be a share for me too from that, for I shall endure the vast churning caused by the whirling of Mandara."
t.1.16.10: And the gods and asuras said to Akūpāra, the king of tortoises: "You should become the support of this mountain."
t.1.16.12: Making Mount Mandara the churning stick and Vāsuki likewise the churning rope, the gods, seeking the amṛta, then began to churn the ocean, the treasury of the waters, together with the Daityas and Dānavas, O brahmin.
t.1.16.11: Saying “So be it,” the tortoise offered his back to bear it, and Indra pressed down the summit of that mountain with a device.
t.1.16.13: The great Asuras clung to one end of the king of the Nāgas, while the gods, all together, stood where the tail was.
t.1.16.15: Then, as the serpent Vāsuki was violently pulled by the gods, winds laden with smoke and flames burst again and again from his mouth.
t.1.16.14: The blessed god Ananta, on the side where Nārāyaṇa stood, lifted the serpent's head and flung it down again and again.
t.1.16.16: Those masses of smoke, turned into masses of clouds charged with lightning, rained down upon the hosts of gods, who were worn out by fatigue and heat.
t.1.16.17: And from the summit of that mountain peak, showers of flowers fell down and covered the hosts of gods and asuras on every side with garlands.
t.1.16.18: Then there arose a mighty roar, like the thundering of great clouds, from the ocean as it was being churned with Mandara by the gods and the asuras.
t.1.16.19: There, crushed by the great mountain, various aquatic creatures by the hundreds met their destruction in the salty ocean.
t.1.16.20: And the mountain brought to destruction the various creatures of the waters, those dwelling in the depths of Pātāla.
t.1.16.21: And as that mountain was being whirled about, great trees full of birds, grinding against one another, fell from the mountain's summit.
t.1.16.22: And the fire born of their friction, blazing again and again with its flames, enveloped Mount Mandara as a dark cloud is enveloped by lightning.
t.1.16.24: Then Indra, best of the immortals, quenched on every side, with water born of the clouds, that fire which was burning here and there.
t.1.16.23: The fire burned the elephants and the lions that had rushed out, and all the various creatures too, leaving them lifeless.
t.1.16.25: Then many kinds of resins of the great trees, and the abundant juices of herbs, flowed there into the waters of the ocean.
t.1.16.26: By the milky essence of those saps, whose potency was that of amṛta, and by the outflow of the gold, the gods attained immortality.
t.1.16.27: Then the water of that ocean, mingled with the finest juices, became milk, and from that milk there came forth ghee.
t.1.16.28: Then the gods said to Brahmā, the giver of boons, who was seated there: "We are utterly exhausted, O Brahman, and yet that amṛta does not arise."
t.1.16.30: Then Brahmā spoke these words to the god Nārāyaṇa: "Grant them strength, O Viṣṇu; you are the final refuge in this matter."
t.1.16.29: All but the god Nārāyaṇa are weary, the Daityas and likewise the foremost of the Nāgas, and this churning of the ocean, too, was begun long ago.
t.1.16.31: I give strength to all who have undertaken this task. Let the pitcher be churned by all, let Mandara be turned round.
t.1.16.32: Having heard the words of Nārāyaṇa, those mighty ones, acting together, once again violently churned the waters of the great ocean into turmoil.
t.1.16.34: Immediately after, from the clarified butter arose Śrī, clad in white garments; the goddess Surā arose, and likewise the white horse.
t.1.16.33: Then from the ocean arose Soma, the cool-rayed moon, blazing and of serene radiance, as if equal to the sun of a hundred thousand rays.
t.1.16.35: And the divine jewel Kaustubha arose, born of the amṛta, glorious and blazing with rays of light, and it came to rest upon the breast of Nārāyaṇa.
t.1.16.37: Then the god Dhanvantari rose up, embodied in beautiful form, bearing a white water-pot in which the amṛta rests.
t.1.16.36: Śrī, Surā, Soma, and the steed swift as thought went to where the gods were, keeping to the path of the sun.
t.1.16.38: Seeing this most wondrous thing, a great clamor arose over the amṛta from the Dānavas, who were crying out, "This is mine!"
t.1.16.39: Then the lord Nārāyaṇa, resorting to his bewitching māyā and assuming the wondrous form of a woman, approached the Dānavas.
t.1.16.40: Then the Dānavas and Daiteyas, all of them deluded in mind, their hearts fixed upon her, gave that amṛta to that woman.
